title.en: A river, a hill and a tree

text.en: A pilgrim walks for days to a hilltop shrine, bathes in a river on the way and rests under a peepal tree. For the pilgrim, the river, the hill and the tree are all sacred. In India the land itself is seen as sacred, not only a building or a book. In this chapter we ask how and why places become sacred and what that means for us.

A sacred place is one connected with a religion, a spiritual figure or something larger than ordinary worldly life. But sacredness is not only about religion: it also connects with geography, traditions and, in India, with a view of the whole of nature as sacred. Followers of other faiths often visit such places too, for example the Dargah Sharif of Ajmer in Rajasthan and the Velankanni Church in Tamil Nadu. Bodh Gaya receives more than four million visitors every year.
A tirtha is a holy place, literally a crossing place, a ford where one crosses over. In the Jain tradition a tirtha is linked to places where the Tirthankaras attained liberation or where major events of their lives occurred; a Tirthankara is one who makes a tirtha. Badrinath, Kedarnath and Amarnath high in the snowy Himalayas and Kanyakumari in the south show how pilgrimage places cover the whole country. The tradition of pilgrimage is not only a physical journey but an inner journey that needs a code of conduct. Wari is a pilgrimage held regularly, in this case yearly, such as the Pandharpur wari in Maharashtra.
Each shrine has its own mythology. A legend tells of Shiva carrying the body of Sati in grief, and her body parts fell in many places that became Shakti Peethas. Such stories link far-off places into networks. The four Char Dham, Badrinath, Dwarka, Puri and Rameswaram, are a famous network. There are many more regional ones. These networks crisscross India and form a sacred geography that unites its length and breadth. The Niyam Dongar hill in Odisha is sacred to the Dongria Khond tribe, showing that tribal beliefs are part of this geography. The landscape itself is seen as sacred space, or punyakshetra.
The Nadistuti Sukta of the Rig Veda praises rivers and invokes 19 major rivers of ancient northwest India. Rivers such as the Ganga are worshipped as mothers. The Kumbh Mela originates in the legend of amrita manthana, the churning of the ocean. It is held in turn at Prayagraj, Haridwar, Ujjain and Nashik, and Prayagraj hosts the Kumbh every six years in the form of the Ardh Kumbh. A dip in the river at a prescribed time is considered most auspicious. Many tirthas and temples are on hilltops, for the physical climb is seen as a symbolic journey to the divine. The peepal tree, botanically Ficus religiosa, the sacred fig, stays green almost all year and gives food and shelter to many birds and animals. Sacred groves are often home to small water bodies and help in water conservation, and bats help in pollination and seed dispersal.
People travelled for different reasons, to worship, to trade, to learn, but their routes often overlapped. Uttarapatha connected the north-west and the east, and Dakshinapatha ran from Kaushambi through Ujjain to Pratishthana (Paithan). Ancient Greece had sacred mountains and groves too, so the idea is shared by many cultures, though India has kept it alive for thousands of years.
A harmonious relation between people and the sacred geography sustained Indian civilisation over millennia and created shared values across the Subcontinent. Today sacred places are being polluted by neglect and lack of care. If air, water, land, trees and mountains are sacred, then we must act to restore and conserve them.

problem.en: Show how a sacred tree helps nature as well as people.

text.en: A peepal tree stays green most of the year.
It feeds and shelters birds and animals.
Sacred groves also store water and bats pollinate and spread seeds, so the belief protects biodiversity.

prompt.en: Why do people visit a tirtha and how do pilgrimages help unite India?

requiredIdeas.en: For worship, merit and an inner spiritual journey.
Networks like the Char Dham link all regions.
Pilgrim and trade routes overlap, spreading ideas.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking sacredness is only about temples.
Thinking only one religion has sacred places.

points.en: In India land, rivers, mountains and trees are seen as sacred.
Tirthas and pilgrimages form networks across the country.
The Kumbh Mela and Char Dham are examples.
Sacred groves and trees help conserve nature; we must protect sacred places.
